$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨3,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(3,1).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(3,1)-f(0,0) \\  & =({3}^{3}+1)-({0}^{3}+0) \\  & =(27+1)-0 \\  & =28.\end{aligned}

Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨e,2,e^{-1}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,1,1)$ and $(e,2,e^{-1}).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(1))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(e,2,e^{-1})-f(1,1,1) \\  & =\left(- 2 \left(e\right) \left(2\right)^{2} + \left(e\right) \left(2\right) \left(e^{-1}\right)\right)-\left(- 2 \left(1\right) \left(1\right)^{2} + \left(1\right) \left(1\right) \left(1\right)\right) \\  & =\left(2 - 8 e\right)-\left(-1\right) \\  & =3 - 8 e.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=3 x y^{2} - 3 x y z.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $r(t)=⟨e^{t},t + 2,e^{- t}⟩$ for $t\in [0,2],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨1,2,1⟩ \\ r(2) & =⟨e^{2},4,e^{-2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,2,1)$ and $(e^{2},4,e^{-2}).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(2))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(e^{2},4,e^{-2})-f(1,2,1) \\  & =\left(3 \left(e^{2}\right) \left(4\right)^{2} - 3 \left(e^{2}\right) \left(4\right) \left(e^{-2}\right)\right)-\left(3 \left(1\right) \left(2\right)^{2} - 3 \left(1\right) \left(2\right) \left(1\right)\right) \\  & =\left(-12 + 48 e^{2}\right)-\left(6\right) \\  & =-18 + 48 e^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
